title: Recomp guide (part. 2): Who can do it & diet manipulation
summary: Part 2 of his recomp guide: who should recomp (best suited to experienced naturals happy with their size who want to redistribute mass, not skinny beginners or very overweight people) and how to handle diet. Keep bodyweight constant, fix diet and training variables before starting, raise calories as muscle is gained, and don't rely on appetite alone. He illustrates with his own weight history and dropping dairy.

claims.claim: Anyone can recomp, but starting body composition decides whether you should attempt it.
A recomp trades fat for muscle, so it's very hard for skinny people with little muscle or fat; there's nothing to trade.
For skinny men like he used to be, he prefers a slow bulk on clean whole foods; dirty bulks only for the truly desperate, and he doesn't advise them.
Beginners should just eat and gain weight (unless very overweight) rather than worry about recomping.
Very overweight people can recomp easily but it's slow; a cut gets as good muscle gains with far more fat loss, because with that much fat the body won't starve the muscles.

The ideal recomp candidate is a natural lifter who has done many bulk/cut cycles, is happy with their overall size, and wants to redistribute mass; they have fat to trade, a strength base, and know how their strength fluctuates.
Apart from a small cut to prep for something like an online bodybuilding contest, he doesn't see himself doing bulk and cut cycles again; he believes recomping is the future.
In a recomp diet and training are equally important: training gauges whether it's working, diet drives the results faster, and appetite acts as a gauge too.

His weight history: slowly bulked to 240 lbs and got too fat, panicked and crash-cut to 210 losing muscle, panicked again from body dysmorphia and bulked fast to 225, then slowly cut to about 215 and started recomping.
His repeated up-and-down bulks and cuts harmed his body: his fat distribution went haywire and he got fat deposits in places he never had them.

After dropping dairy and cutting red meat in January he went from 215 to 210 lbs in about two months, but looked much leaner, mostly from losing water and puffiness (face, love handles), which he links to estrogen in the diet.
Recomp at a stable bodyweight, and don't make big diet changes just before or early in the recomp; your body takes time to catch up and a big change confounds the results.
Don't change your training mid-recomp either; changing variables makes it impossible to attribute results.

Once protein, fats and carbs needs are met, how you fill remaining calories is individual; his body does great on carbs and he gets leaner eating them, and he thinks swapping carbs for fats at the same bodyweight would slow his fat loss.
Experiment with your diet before the recomp, not during it.
As a recomp succeeds, calories must rise: muscle is more metabolically costly than fat, so if you don't match the small metabolic increase you'll slide into a slow cut.
Avoid zigzagging micro-bulks and micro-cuts around the target weight; the point is to show the body it can stay the same weight, gain strength and improve muscularly.

He has a slow metabolism, does well on low calories and has a normal appetite; after dropping dairy his appetite didn't make up the lost calories, he lost weight, and he noticed because some lifts regressed.
Don't rely solely on appetite during a recomp; his own advice to eat instinctively without counting backfired on him.
To maintain 210-211 lbs while getting stronger, he forces one daily snack of about 300 kcal when slightly hungry to avoid a deficit.
Don't follow someone else's diet for years; experiment. Dropping dairy was a revolution for him, and eating garlic and onions really helped him.
He reports great recomp results: his physique is getting cleaner and leaner, with some measurements going up and some stagnating.
A calorie is not just a calorie: the macro source and timing (e.g. protein with carbs) affect insulin and where the body puts calories, so macro changes alter fat distribution.

During a recomp the only diet change should be a gradual calorie increase as muscle is gained, and the only training change a small tonnage increase; you recomp through both diet and training equally.
